newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Q3 growth seen strong but Q4 likely to flag.
newsitem.headline: French Q3 growth seen strong but Q4 likely to flag.

text.p: France is expected to report robust third-quarter economic growth on Thursday, boosted by a rush to buy cars ahead of the end to a state subsidy scheme, but the good news will be offset by prospects of a weak final quarter.

"The big help in the third quarter is going to come from households buying cars," economist Steven Englander of Smith Barney said on Wednesday. "When we get to the fourth quarter, the economy is going to be left to its own resources."
Third-quarter GDP was expected to show a rise of 0.9 percent from the second quarter, according to a median forecast of 10 economists polled by Reuters. The range was 0.7 percent to 1.3.

Economists said the big contributor to third-quarter growth would come from a consumer scramble to profit from a state car buying subsidy which ended September 30. The numbers would also be flattered by a 0.4 percent fall in second quarter growth.
A firm trade peformance was also seen helping.

Economists said they did not expect the strong third quarter data to prompt the Bank of France to cut interest rates after its monetary policy council meeting on Thursday -- especially given the latest row over France's strong franc policy.
"They won't cut rates with all the calls for an aggressive easing of the monetary stance," said David Naude of JP Morgan.
Former French president Valery Giscard D'Estaing renewed on Tuesday his appeal for a weaker franc, saying it would revive the sluggish economy.
A harbinger of a gloomier fourth quarter came on Tuesday with figures showing consumer spending on manufactured goods fell a bigger-than-expected 2.6 percent in October.
Economists said not all of the fall could be explained by the plunge in car buying after the expiry of the subsidy scheme. Consumers remained wary in the face of record 12.6 unemployment.
"Everthing's been going down, consumer spending, industrial production. There's not much momentum," said Naude.
Economists said the economy was recovering but the pace had been hampered by weak investment and destocking amid business scepticism about future demand prospects.
"It is a very gentle recovery, weaker than other European recoveries," said Robert Prior of HSBC James Capel.

The centre-right government has been banking on a revival in consumer spending and corporate investment to boost growth to 2.3 percent next year from a forecast 1.3 percent this year and help it cut the deficit to qualify for European monetary union.
